question: Can capacity-dependent feature coverage explain why larger language models follow corrupted in-context examples more strongly than smaller models?

key_findings.claim: For the stylized linear-regression learner, a rank constraint makes the population-optimal attention map retain only the highest-variance covariance directions.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 4.1 diagonalizes the token covariance and gives a truncated closed-form solution: rank r keeps the first r eigenvectors, while the full-rank solution covers all directions. Rank of the merged key-query matrix is used as the model-size surrogate.

key_findings.claim: The regression theory predicts a noise cost from extra rank only after assuming that the smaller model already spans every useful evaluation direction.
key_findings.evidence: The general loss in Theorem 4.2 contains both missed-signal and retained-noise terms, so increasing rank can help or hurt. The monotone larger-is-worse conclusion in Theorem 4.3 imposes w=Qs, eliminating useful residual signal beyond rank r; each added direction then contributes only finite-context and label-noise error.

key_findings.claim: In the sparse-parity construction, increasing head count adds exact pattern-covering neurons for rare feature pairs while preserving a smaller important-feature subnetwork.
key_findings.evidence: Under an orthonormal dictionary, correlated binary features, vanishing regularization, infinite context, and a strict upper bound on rare-task probability, Theorem 5.1 constructs 2(log2 k+1) heads for important pairs and 2(log2 d+1) for all pairs. The proof reduces hinge loss to weighted coverage of signed pair patterns.

key_findings.claim: The parity robustness result compares projected noise energy, not end-to-end classification error under arbitrary corruption.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 5.2 decomposes a clean important-pair query into a shared signal plus projections of finite-sample noise onto small and large feature subspaces; the expected squared projection ratio is (nu1+1)/(nu2+1). Both models have zero hinge loss on the ideal signal, but the theorem does not turn the projection ratio into a general misclassification bound.

key_findings.claim: Llama-family experiments show that larger models more readily reverse their predictions when demonstration labels are flipped, but this can also indicate stronger task learning rather than simple distraction.
key_findings.evidence: Across five binary datasets, 3B–70B base/chat models receive 16 demonstrations with 0–100% label inversion. Larger models begin with better clean accuracy and usually decline more as flips increase; smaller models often remain near a pretraining-biased prediction. The test labels remain clean, so the paper scores adherence to the corrupted mapping as error.

key_findings.claim: The attention-map ablation is correlational and too narrow to validate the proposed feature-selection mechanism.
key_findings.evidence: On 100 SST-2 prompts with a concatenated irrelevant sentence, last-layer attention-row norms show Llama-2-13B attending mainly to relevant text and 70B attending to both. Attention magnitude is neither a causal contribution measure nor aligned to the covariance eigenfeatures or parity neurons in the theory.

method.core_idea: Model scale as the number of feature directions or parity patterns an idealized transformer can cover, then show that extra coverage raises noise sensitivity when all additional features are irrelevant at evaluation.
method.mechanism: The paper solves two population objectives in closed form: rank-constrained one-layer linear self-attention on Gaussian regression and head-constrained two-layer ReLU attention on sparse parity. It derives signal/noise decompositions for their optimal predictors and compares those predictions with label-flip and irrelevant-sentence behavior in Llama and Llama-2 models.
assumptions: Merged key-query rank or attention-head count is a useful proxy for language-model parameter scale.
High-variance pretraining directions are the important evaluation features, and the smaller model already covers the useful subset in the monotone result.
Regression prompts follow Gaussian linear tasks and population-optimal training rather than finite nonconvex optimization.
Parity features form an orthonormal dictionary with a prescribed label correlation and an extremely small rare-task rate.
Infinite-context, vanishing-weight-decay parity optima describe finite-context pretrained language models.
Flipped natural-language labels are noise rather than an intentionally redefined in-context task.

techniques.role: Represents model scale by the rank of the merged key-query map in linear attention.
Solves the low-rank population objective by retaining leading covariance eigenvectors.
Constructs ReLU attention heads as signed binary codes that cover parity-feature pairs.
Separates missed useful directions from finite-context and corrupted-label contributions.
Measures how model-family scale changes adherence to corrupted in-context mappings.
Compares last-layer attention norms from labels to relevant and irrelevant sentences.

evaluations.setting: Closed-form Gaussian linear-regression ICL with one-layer, one-head linear attention.
evaluations.metric: Expected squared query error under finite-context input and label noise.
evaluations.result: Extra rank helps by covering residual signal in the general result but strictly hurts when all new directions contain only noise.
evaluations.baseline: Population-optimal rank-r versus rank-r-prime attention maps.

evaluations.setting: Sparse two-feature parity ICL with a two-layer multi-head ReLU transformer.
evaluations.metric: Hinge loss and expected projected noise energy.
evaluations.result: The smaller optimum covers frequent feature pairs; the larger optimum covers all pairs and receives proportionally more projected finite-sample noise on frequent-pair tests.

evaluations.setting: RTE, SST-2, QQP, WNLI, and SUBJ with 16 label-corrupted demonstrations.
evaluations.metric: Accuracy over 1,000 prompts per dataset, five runs, across flip fractions.
evaluations.result: The 70B variants generally lose more accuracy as labels flip, while smaller variants change less and often remain near their pretrained semantic bias.
evaluations.baseline: Llama/Llama-2 3B, 7B, 13B, and 70B base or chat variants plus random accuracy.

evaluations.setting: SST-2 prompts concatenated with irrelevant GSM-IC sentences.
evaluations.metric: Norm of the final attention-map row between label tokens and sentence tokens over 100 prompts.
evaluations.result: Llama-2-13B shows higher correlation with relevant than irrelevant text; 70B attends appreciably to both.
evaluations.baseline: 13B versus 70B and original versus flipped labels.

limitations: Author-stated: the stylized closed-form analysis does not extend easily to multilayer nonconvex transformers and omits optimization trajectories.
Author-stated: empirical validation uses simple binary classification and remains far from practical open-ended LLM use.
Reviewer inference: rank and head count are changed in isolation, while real scaling changes width, depth, data, training compute, tokenization, and alignment together.
Reviewer inference: the larger-is-less-robust theorem assumes extra capacity covers only nuisance features; it does not predict settings where capacity separates signal from noise better.
Reviewer inference: Llama checkpoints differ by family and instruction tuning, and no controlled same-data scaling suite isolates parameter count.
Reviewer inference: the main natural-language evidence conflates harmful corruption with the capability to infer a novel input-label mapping.
Reviewer inference: last-layer attention norms are not causal explanations and do not test the theory's latent features.
failure_modes: A deployment treats valid task redefinition as noise and disables the larger model's useful contextual adaptation.
A smaller model appears robust only because it ignores demonstrations and falls back to a memorized label prior.
Extra capacity learns a denoising or consistency-checking algorithm, reversing the predicted scale trend.
Noise is structured, query-dependent, or semantically detectable rather than isotropic in unused feature directions.
Prompt format, label-token priors, or instruction tuning dominates the effect attributed to capacity.
Attention probes highlight tokens without measuring their effect on logits or counterfactual decisions.
reusable_insights: Any scale-versus-robustness claim should separate contextual task-learning strength from susceptibility to genuinely erroneous evidence.
Feature coverage creates a bias-variance tradeoff only relative to a stated evaluation distribution; added dimensions are not intrinsically noise.
Controlled scaling studies should hold training data, tokenizer, architecture family, prompt, and alignment constant and report zero-shot as well as task-learning baselines.
Mechanistic theory gains credibility when its latent variables can be intervened on in the real model, not merely correlated with attention maps.
Risk-controlled ICL can use the zero-shot predictor as a fallback when demonstrations fail a reliability test.
open_questions: Under controlled pretraining, when does added width or depth learn explicit outlier rejection rather than indiscriminate extra feature coverage?
Can causal subspace interventions connect real LLM scale to the covariance directions or pattern-covering heads in the theory?
How should an evaluator distinguish corrupted demonstrations from a legitimate remapping task with unfamiliar labels?
Does the scale trend persist for generation, reasoning, multilingual, and agent trajectories under calibrated semantic corruption?
Can finite-sample theory select an optimal effective rank or early-exit depth from prompt reliability?
Do later layerwise-compression or low-frequency accounts explain noise robustness better across modern architectures?

competitive_landscape.title: Larger Language Models Do In-Context Learning Differently
competitive_landscape.difference: Wei et al. establish the label-flip scale phenomenon across models and motivate the reviewed paper; the reviewed work adds two closed-form feature-coverage explanations and a small attention probe.

competitive_landscape.title: Exploring the Robustness of In-Context Learning with Noisy Labels
competitive_landscape.difference: Cheng et al. train controlled GPT-2 transformers on several synthetic function classes and find substantial noisy-label resilience, including benefits from noise-augmented pretraining; they study robustness across size without the reviewed paper's feature-truncation optimum.

competitive_landscape.title: On the Noise Robustness of In-Context Learning for Text Generation
competitive_landscape.difference: Gao et al. show that noisy demonstrations can strongly damage generation and propose local-perplexity replacement, extending beyond the reviewed paper's binary classification and explaining robustness through selection rather than model scale.

competitive_landscape.title: Too Big to Fool: Resisting Deception in Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: This evaluation reports larger models as more resilient to misleading prompts and better at using truthful hints, showing that the scale trend reverses when the context permits truth discrimination rather than arbitrary label remapping.

competitive_landscape.title: Safe and Efficient In-Context Learning via Risk Control
competitive_landscape.difference: Wynn et al. use distribution-free risk control and dynamic early exits to bound degradation below zero-shot behavior, operationalizing a defense instead of treating smaller capacity as inherently safer.

competitive_landscape.title: From Compression to Expression: A Layerwise Analysis of In-Context Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Jiang et al. analyze task-information compression and later-layer expression across architectures and connect larger scale to improved ICL and noisy-example robustness, offering a different internal geometry than fixed feature overcoverage.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Closed-form optimal transformers explain the observed model-scale difference: small models prioritize important hidden features, while large models cover more features and therefore absorb more contextual noise.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper derives spectral and combinatorial optima, proves conditional signal/noise decompositions, and observes matching label-flip and attention trends in Llama-family checkpoints.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The paired regression/parity derivations are a substantive theoretical contribution, especially the explicit pattern-covering construction. The bridge to real scale is weak: capacity proxies, optimality assumptions, and nuisance-only added features encode much of the conclusion. Concurrent and later work finds both robustness and reverse scale trends under different noise semantics. The narrow novelty is a conditional feature-coverage account, not a general law that larger language models are more distractible.

reviewer_notes: Read all 23 extracted pages, including both complete proofs and the stated limitations. Visually inspected Theorems 4.1 and 5.2 plus all three empirical figures; the plotted scale trend is real but heterogeneous by dataset, checkpoint, and flip level. The PMLR record lists PDF and OpenReview material but no first-party code artifact, so no code audit was possible. Current primary arXiv and OpenReview competitors were checked on 2026-08-23.
